source.title: Beyond neural scaling laws: beating power law scaling via data pruning
source.authors: Ben Sorscher; Robert Geirhos; Shashank Shekhar; S. Ganguli; Ari S. Morcos

record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior under data pruning and reports image-model results that depart from power-law scaling, as well as conditions under which that departure changes.
record.gate_note: The study's own relevant results concern test error or accuracy in vision models and a teacher-student perceptron, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. Language-model scaling laws and compute-optimal allocations are discussed as background or cited results, not tested here.
record.test_reason: The study gives its own results on image models (ResNet18/50 trained from scratch, ViT fine-tuning) and a perceptron theory. Unpruned curves (f=1) follow labelled power laws in test error. Pareto-optimal pruned curves beat a power law, and imperfect pruning metrics cause a crossover back to power law. This bears on V5 (image modality and fine-tuning) and on V7 (curves bending away from a single power law depending on data setup). It does not test language-model loss, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, shape or downstream predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points. The better-than-power-law Pareto frontier requires pruning more aggressively from larger initial datasets. Fixed-fraction pruning still yields power-law scaling. The authors also present a self-supervised prototype metric that matches the best supervised metric, enabling 20% of ImageNet to be discarded.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and measures vision-model test error and perceptron generalization under data pruning, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling or parameter/token/compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Pruning metric quality and probe training duration change whether the reported envelope crosses over to a power law; the paper also reports metric-dependent scaling curves and discusses class balancing and training duration as performance factors.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning upstream ImageNet pretraining data can preserve downstream CIFAR-10 performance after fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this ResNet50 transfer setup, pre-training on a pruned ImageNet subset as small as 50% can match or exceed downstream performance from full-ImageNet pretraining.

record.problems: The study does not test language models or the language-model loss and allocation claims. Several scaling results are presented in figures without exact curve values or fit statistics in the text. Its image-model departures from power laws are obtained with data pruning, and the authors note that high-quality pruning metrics and class balancing are important.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the other ImageNet pruning-metric benchmark results and auxiliary pruning curves in Figures 5 and 9 because they report metric comparisons or related pruning results rather than additional separately quantified scaling outcomes. Also omitted compute and OOD results that do not test the listed loss-scaling versions.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss sweeps.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: architecture shape is not varied.
Model-size and compute scaling in vision (only dataset size is varied; App. C compute is preliminary). Video, repeated data, other modalities. Fitted exponents are not reported in the text.
All: downstream predictability from scale or loss is not studied.
Parameter counting, training schedule, fitting-method disagreement across published laws, and compute-optimal split estimates.

missing.what: Unpruned (f=1) power-law fits to test error versus dataset size in each vision setting, and the verified prediction that fixed-f pruning reverts to power law with the random-pruning exponent.

ImageNet scaling with EL2N (0% and 50% class balancing) and self-supervised prototypes shows weaker departures from power law than memorization. This is a metric-dependence result on curve shape; rows_left_out declares it only as metric comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label for V5 is too strong. The study itself reproduces power-law scaling for random data and shows the departure only under deliberate Pareto-optimal data selection. That makes it a scope limit on V5, not a refutation. All measures are classification test error, not cross-entropy loss. Most curve evidence is figure only, with no exponents or fit statistics in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute, including how either quantity grows with compute.
The effect of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

Image models and one fine-tuning setting are tested under data pruning. The study does not test video models, repeated data, language models, or the generality of a power-law form across modalities and regimes without pruning.
Whether downstream task performance improves predictably with model scale or pretraining loss.

The study tests departures from a single power law and sensitivity to pruning setup or metric quality. It does not compare published language-model exponents, parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods for those laws, or compute-optimal allocation estimates.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Measured test error across pruned CIFAR-10 dataset sizes using EL2N scores.
rows.measure: Test error versus pruned dataset size
rows.baseline: figure only; the no-pruning curve (f = 1) is labelled with its best-fit power law
rows.value: figure only; the text reports better-than-power-law scaling at larger initial dataset sizes and more aggressive pruning
rows.note: The stated result is for data selected by pruning, not random selection.
rows.check: 'reversed' is wrong: error falling faster than a power law is not the opposite effect. The f=1 curve follows a labelled power law, and the authors say fixed-f curves return to power law. Only the Pareto frontier across initial size and pruning fraction departs. Figure only.

rows.subject: ViT
rows.operation_detail: Measured CIFAR-10 performance while fine-tuning on EL2N-pruned subsets.
rows.measure: CIFAR-10 performance versus fine-tuning dataset size
rows.baseline: Fine-tuning on all of CIFAR-10; numeric value not stated in text
rows.value: Fine-tuning on 10% of CIFAR-10 can match or exceed performance with all of CIFAR-10; the authors describe this as beating power-law scaling in fine-tuning

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Measured the test-error envelope after pruning using a weak EL2N metric from a probe trained for 4 epochs.
rows.measure: Test-error envelope versus pruned dataset size
rows.value: figure only; the text states that the learning-curve envelope is lower-bounded by a power law at some fmin
rows.note: The authors characterize this as the weak-metric case predicted to cross over to power-law behavior.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Measured the test-error envelope after pruning using a stronger EL2N metric from a probe trained for 40 epochs.
rows.measure: Test-error envelope versus pruned dataset size
rows.value: figure only; the text states that the learning curve can break through the power-law lower bound
rows.note: Together with R5, this shows that probe training duration changes the reported scaling envelope.
rows.check: Figure only. The R5 vs R6 contrast is the result: probe duration determines whether the envelope stays power-law bounded.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared least-squares power-law and exponential fits to an empirically estimated Pareto frontier.

conditions.value: estimated using 300 additional models around the frontier

rows.measure: Fit of test-error Pareto frontier against training examples
rows.baseline: Power-law fit by least squares; numerical fit statistic not stated
rows.value: The exponential fit is reported to fit the empirical frontier much better; the authors say the scaling is at least exponential
rows.note: The text gives no numerical goodness-of-fit values.
rows.check: No goodness-of-fit numbers are given. The fit is to a pruned Pareto frontier, not to random-data scaling.

rows.subject: Perceptron in teacher-student setting
rows.operation_detail: Analytically derived and simulated test-error scaling under Pareto-optimal data pruning with a perfect teacher-aligned pruning metric.

conditions.value: Pareto optimal over initial dataset size and fraction retained

rows.measure: Test error versus pruned dataset size
rows.baseline: Random/no-pruning scaling is described as the classical power law ε ∝ αprune^-1
rows.value: The Pareto frontier is described as tracing at least an exponential scaling law; Figure 11A compares power-law, exponential, factorial, and iterated-factorial fits
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over 100 independent draws of teacher and training examples
rows.note: The analytic theory and numerical simulations are reported to match well.
rows.check: Toy perceptron theory and simulation, not a neural network trained on real data. Treat as mechanistic support only.

rows.subject: Perceptron in teacher-student setting

rows.note: The 24% figure is the stated minimum retained fraction for θ = 10°.
rows.check: Toy perceptron. The 24% figure is an asymptotic minimum retained fraction from theory.

relationships.condition: Unpruned (f=1, i.e. random) training sets for ResNet18 on CIFAR-10/SVHN and ResNet50 on ImageNet
relationships.reason: From the text, not a row: Fig. 3's f=1 curves are 'labeled with their best-fit power law scaling'. Fixed-f curves are said to settle into power law with the random-pruning exponent. Exponents are figure only. Rows R1–R3 cite these curves only as baselines.
relationships.display_finding: Unpruned learning curves followed fitted power laws, while fixed pruning fractions eventually approached power laws with the random-pruning exponent.

source_check.condition: Unpruned (f=1, i.e. random) training sets for ResNet18 on CIFAR-10/SVHN and ResNet50 on ImageNet
source_check.reason: Figure 3 explicitly identifies best-fit power-law scaling for the unpruned baselines accompanying R1–R3; SVHN uses error after subtracting its 1.1% asymptote.

relationships.condition: Training or fine-tuning sets chosen by a strong pruning metric, with the pruning fraction tuned to initial dataset size (Pareto frontier)
relationships.reason: Under Pareto-optimal pruning, test error versus pruned dataset size falls faster than a power law. This holds for ResNets from scratch (R1–R3) and ViT fine-tuning (R4). So the power-law form depends on data being randomly sampled.
relationships.display_finding: Test error decreased faster than a power law along the optimal pruning frontier for both ResNets trained from scratch and fine-tuned ViTs.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Training or fine-tuning sets chosen by a strong pruning metric, with the pruning fraction tuned to initial dataset size (Pareto frontier)
source_check.reason: R1–R4 show faster-than-power-law behavior under tuned pruning, while unpruned and fixed-fraction regimes retain power-law behavior. This qualifies the scaling form by data-selection regime.

relationships.condition: Data-pruned regimes: ResNet18 on SVHN (R5–R7) and teacher-student perceptron theory (R8–R10)
relationships.reason: The curve shape depends on how the data are selected. A weak 4-epoch probe keeps the envelope power-law bounded, while a 40-epoch probe breaks through (R5, R6). An exponential fits the SVHN frontier better than a power law (R7). Perceptron theory gives an exponential-then-power-law crossover set by metric angle (R8–R10).
relationships.display_finding: A 4-epoch probe leaves the pruning envelope bounded by a power law, whereas a 40-epoch probe surpasses it; an exponential better fits the SVHN frontier, and perceptron theory predicts an exponential-to-power-law crossover governed by metric angle.

tranche.reason: Its theoretical and empirical results qualify power-law scaling by showing faster scaling under optimized data selection and a return to power-law behavior with imperfect pruning metrics.

statements.correction: Unpruned ResNet curves: best-fit power laws. Fixed-fraction pruning: asymptotic power-law scaling. Pareto-optimal pruning with increasingly aggressive selection: faster-than-power-law scaling for from-scratch ResNets and fine-tuned ViTs. V5 verdict for tuned pruning: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The pruning result attributed to this study is accurate, but the challenges label overstates the mixed, condition-dependent evidence: unpruned and fixed-fraction regimes retain power-law scaling.
